chunks: From al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from 'Uqbah ibn Ja'far, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who transfers another man's money to a money-changer (sarraf), and then the condition of the money-changer changes (becomes insolvent). Does he go back to the owner (of the money) if he (the owner) acted prudently and was satisfied (with the transfer)? He said, 'No.'

key_terms.احْتَالَ: He acted prudently or with due diligence
key_terms.رَضِيَ: He was satisfied or content with the transaction
key_terms.يَتَغَيَّرُ حَالُهُ: His condition changes, specifically referring to insolvency or bankruptcy
key_terms.يَرْجِعُ: To go back or claim recourse
key_terms.يُحِيلُ: To transfer a debt or money to a third party

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a transferred debt if the recipient becomes insolvent?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith from Imam al-Rida (AS) establishes a key principle in Shia commercial jurisprudence regarding *hiyalah* (debt transfer). It clarifies that if the transferor (*mu'il*) selects the money-changer (*sarrafi*) and accepts the arrangement, the risk of the money-changer's subsequent insolvency falls on the transferor, not the original debtor, provided the transferor acted with due diligence (*ihtilal*) and consent. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on contractual autonomy and the allocation of risk based on the parties' active choices in financial transactions.
